citations.quote:
Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

For every $n\ge0$,
$$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}(f^\lambda)^2=n!,$$
where $f^\lambda$ is the number of standard $\lambda$-tableaux and
$f^\varnothing=1$, $0!=1$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$\alpha,\nu\vdash n$ be partitions of $n$ with conjugate $\nu'$ and
$x_\alpha,y_\nu\in H_{R,q}(S_n)$ as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]. If $\alpha$
is not dominated by $\nu'$ in the sense of
[[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]], that is, if
$\sum_{i\le k}\alpha_i>\sum_{i\le k}\nu'_i$ for some $k\ge1$, then
$$x_\alpha Hy_\nu=0.$$
The vanishing is a universal Laurent-polynomial identity, remains valid at
singular parameters and uses no cancellation of $q+1$. The proof explicitly
sorts parabolic double cosets and uses the zero product
$(1+T_i)(1-q^{-1}T_i)=0$. Empty shapes and $n=0,1$ are included. No choice
principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: **Compositions.** A composition of $n$ is a finite sequence $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ of nonnegative integers with $\sum\alpha_i=n$; its row blocks $B_r$, row group $S_\alpha$, row-filled tableau $t^\alpha$, row-standard tableaux, set $D_\alpha$, distinguished elements $d_\alpha(u)$, and elements $x_\alpha=\sum_{w\in S_\alpha}T_w$, $b_u:=x_\alpha T_{d_\alpha(u)}$ are defined exactly as for partitions in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], and for row-standard $\alpha$-tableaux $s,t$ put $m^\alpha_{st}:=T_{d_\alpha(s)}^*x_\alpha T_{d_\alpha(t)}$, so that $b_t=m^\alpha_{t^\alpha t}$. Every statement of [F2] was proved for partitions but uses only that the row group is a product of symmetric groups on consecutive blocks, so it applies verbatim to compositions.

**Dominance of tableaux by counting.** For $\alpha$-tableaux $u,v$ and integers $m\ge0$, $k\ge1$ put $c_{m,k}(u):=\#\{x\in B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_k:u(x)\le m\}$; write $u\unrhd v$ when $c_{m,k}(u)\ge c_{m,k}(v)$ for all $m,k$, and $u\equiv v$ when all these numbers agree. Passing from $u$ to $u\cdot s_i$ exchanges the labels $i$ and $i+1$, so it changes only the counts at $m=i$, and $c_{i,k}(u\cdot s_i)=c_{i-1,k}(u)+[i+1\text{ lies in the first }k\text{ blocks of }u]$ because the label $i$ is replaced by $i+1$ and all other labels $\le i$ stay put. In particular $u\equiv v$ implies $u\cdot s_i\equiv v\cdot s_i$, and if $u,v$ are both row standard then $u\equiv v$ if and only if $u=v$, because the numbers $c_{m,k}$ determine the multiset of entries of each block and a row-standard tableau is its block multisets sorted increasingly. Suppose now that $s$ is row standard, that $s':=s\cdot s_i$ is row standard, and that the labels $i,i+1$ lie in rows $a<b$ of $s$, so that $s'$ is obtained from $s$ by moving $i$ down into row $b$ and $i+1$ up into row $a$. Then for every row-standard $r$ with $r\unrhd s$ one has $r\unrhd s'$ and $r\cdot s_i\unrhd s'$. Indeed for $m\ne i$ the counts are unchanged by both swaps, so $c_{m,k}(r)\ge c_{m,k}(s)=c_{m,k}(s')$ and the same for $r\cdot s_i$; for $m=i$ one has $c_{i,k}(s')=c_{i-1,k}(s)+[k\ge b]$, while $c_{i,k}(r)\ge c_{i,k}(s)\ge c_{i-1,k}(s)+[k\ge b]=c_{i,k}(s')$ for every $k$, and $c_{i,k}(r\cdot s_i)=c_{i-1,k}(r)+[i+1\text{ lies in the first }k\text{ blocks of }r]\ge c_{i-1,k}(r)\ge c_{i-1,k}(s)=c_{i,k}(s')$ for $k<b$, while for $k\ge b$ the sharper bound $c_{i,k}(r\cdot s_i)\ge c_{i+1,k}(r)-1\ge c_{i+1,k}(s)-1=c_{i-1,k}(s)+1=c_{i,k}(s')$ holds, the first inequality by $[i\text{ lies in the first }k\text{ blocks of }r]\le1$ and the last because both labels then lie in the first $k$ blocks of $s$.

**The trace pairing.** Define $\tau:H\to R$ by $\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$. The multiplication rules give $\tau(T_wT_i)=\tau(T_iT_w)=q\delta_{w,s_i}$ for every $w$ and every generator $T_i$: in the two-case formulas the identity $T_1$ occurs only in the descent case $w=s_i$, with coefficient $q$. Moving generator letters across one another successively gives $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ for all $a,b\in H$, and $\tau(a^*)=\tau(a)$ since $\tau$ is $R$-linear and $*$ permutes the standard basis. Let $B_0$ be the bilinear form defined on the standard basis by $B_0(T_u,T_v):=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$. Every right $s_i$-orbit $\{T_w,T_{ws_i}\}$ has two elements; writing $w$ for the element with $\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1$, right multiplication by $T_i$ on the block spanned by the orbit has matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&q\\1&q-1\end{pmatrix}$, and the restriction of $B_0$ to the block has matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(q^{\ell(w)},q^{\ell(w)+1})$ with $A^{\mathsf T}D=DA$; distinct blocks are orthogonal, so $B_0(xT_i,y)=B_0(x,yT_i)$ for all $x,y\in H$. Iterating along a reduced word $T_u=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_r}$ gives $B_0(T_u,T_v)=B_0(T_1,T_vT_{i_r}\cdots T_{i_1})=B_0(T_1,T_vT_u^*)$, and $B_0(T_1,y)=\tau(y)$ for every $y$ by the definitions; hence $B_0(T_u,T_v)=\tau(T_vT_u^*)=\tau(T_{u^{-1}}T_v)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$. In particular the bilinear form $(a,b)\mapsto\tau(a^*b)$ equals $B_0$ and has diagonal Gram matrix with unit entries $q^{\ell(u)}$ in the standard basis, so it is unimodular.

**The support lemma.** Let $g$ be a row-standard $\alpha$-tableau, let $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_r}$ be a reduced word, put $t:=g\cdot w$ and $g_k:=g\cdot(s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k})$, and assume $\ell(d_\alpha(t))=\ell(d_\alpha(g))+\ell(w)$. If $v$ is a row-standard $\alpha$-tableau with $vhd g$, then every row-standard tableau $u$ whose basis element $b_u$ is involved in $b_vT_w$ satisfies $uhd t$. First, $\ell(d_\alpha(g_k))=\ell(d_\alpha(g))+k$ for every $k$: the triangle inequality gives $\ell(d_\alpha(g))+r=\ell(d_\alpha(t))\le\ell(d_\alpha(g_k))+(r-k)$ and $\ell(d_\alpha(g_k))\le\ell(d_\alpha(g))+k$, and the two inequalities force equality. Hence each step replaces $g_k$ by the row-standard tableau $g_k\cdot s_{i_{k+1}}$ with $\ell(d_\alpha(g_k\cdot s_{i_{k+1}}))=\ell(d_\alpha(g_k))+1$, so the three-case rule of [F2] gives $b_{g_k}T_{i_{k+1}}=b_{g_{k+1}}$: the swapped tableau is row standard and the length increases. The labels $i,i+1$ therefore lie in different rows of $g_k$ (otherwise the swap would stay in one row and the rule would return a multiple of $b_{g_k}$), and since $g_{k+1}$ is row standard with $\ell(d_\alpha(g_k)s_{i_{k+1}})=\ell(d_\alpha(g_k))+1$, the row-reading position of $i$ precedes that of $i+1$, so $i$ lies in a strictly upper row of $g_k$; this is exactly the configuration of step 1.2. We now show by induction on $k$ that every row-standard $u$ with $b_u$ involved in $b_vT_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_k}$ satisfies $u\unrhd g_k$ and $u
ot\equiv g_k$. For $k=0$ we have $v\unrhd g$ and $v
e g$, and $v\equiv g$ would give $g\unrhd v$, so $v
ot\equiv g$. For the step, the action rule of [F2] shows that $b_uT_{i_{k+1}}$ is a combination of $b_u$ and, when $u\cdot s_{i_{k+1}}$ is row standard, $b_{u\cdot s_{i_{k+1}}}$; step 1.2 applied to $s:=g_k$, $s'=g_{k+1}$ gives $u\unrhd g_{k+1}$ and $u\cdot s_{i_{k+1}}\unrhd g_{k+1}$ whenever the swapped tableau is row standard. Neither output is $\equiv g_{k+1}$: if $u\equiv g_{k+1}$ then $u\unrhd g_k\unrhd g_{k+1}\equiv u$ forces $u\equiv g_k$, and if $u\cdot s_{i_{k+1}}\equiv g_{k+1}$ then applying the swap to the two equivalent tableaux gives $u\equiv g_k$, both contradicting the induction hypothesis. At the end $t$ is row standard, so $u\unrhd t$ together with $u
ot\equiv t$ says exactly that $uhd t$.

**Compositions to partitions.** Let $\alpha$ be a composition and $\beta$ the partition obtained by rearranging its parts. Choose $d$ mapping each row block of $\alpha$ onto a row block of $\beta$ of the same size, increasingly; then $d^{-1}$ is increasing on each block of $\alpha$ and of $\beta$, so $d\in D_\alpha$ and $d^{-1}\in D_\beta$, and conjugation by $d$ exchanges $S_\alpha$ and $S_\beta$. Hence $x_\alpha T_d=\sum_{w\in S_\alpha}T_{wd}=\sum_{u\in S_\alpha d}T_u$ and $T_dx_\beta=\sum_{v\in S_\beta}T_{dv}=\sum_{u\in dS_\beta}T_u$, and these agree because $S_\alpha d=d(d^{-1}S_\alpha d)=dS_\beta$. Thus $x_\alpha=T_dx_\beta T_d^{-1}$ and $T_d$ is invertible. Since $Hx_\beta$ is free with basis $\{T_{d_\beta(s)}^*x_\beta\}$ (the star of the basis of $x_\beta H$) and $x_\beta H$ is free with basis $\{x_\beta T_{d_\beta(u)}\}$ by [F2], expanding $T_{d_\alpha(s)}^*T_d$ and $T_d^{-1}T_{d_\alpha(t)}$ expresses $m^\alpha_{st}$ as an $R$-linear combination of $m^\beta_{uv}$ with $u,v$ row standard; all coefficients are Laurent polynomials in $q$, with no quantum factorial inverted.

**The Garnir belt identity.** Let $\rho$ be a partition and $(i,j)$ a node with $j\le\rho_{i+1}$. Let $\alpha$ replace the two consecutive parts $\rho_i,\rho_{i+1}$ by $j-1,\rho_i+1,\rho_{i+1}-j$, deleting zeros; its blocks are those of $\rho$ except that the belt $a,\dots,b$, where $a=t^\rho(i,j)$ and $b=t^\rho(i+1,j)$, is cut into three consecutive blocks of sizes $j-1$, $\rho_i+1$ and $\rho_{i+1}-j$; the middle block is the interval $a,\dots,b$ itself, of size $\rho_i+1=b-a+1$. Put $D:=S_\alpha\cap D_\rho$ and $E:=S_\rho\cap D_\alpha$. Then $$x_\rho\sum_{d\in D}T_d=\sum_{v\in E}T_v^*x_\alpha.$$ Indeed the products $S_\rho\times D\to S_\rho S_\alpha$, $(u,d)\mapsto ud$, and $E\times S_\alpha\to S_\rho S_\alpha$, $(v,u)\mapsto v^{-1}u$, are bijections with length-additive products, because $D\subseteq D_\rho$, $E\subseteq D_\alpha$ and $\ell(u^{-1}v)=\ell(v^{-1}u)$ for all $u\in S_\alpha$, $v\in D_\alpha$; expanding both sides in the standard basis therefore gives $\sum_{w\in S_\rho S_\alpha}T_w$ for the left side and the same sum for the right side, since $T_v^*=T_{v^{-1}}$.

**The Garnir tableau.** With $\rho,\alpha,(i,j)$ as in step 2.3, let $g$ be the row-standard tableau agreeing with $t^\rho$ outside the belt $a,\dots,b$, whose row $i+1$ carries the $j$ smallest belt entries increasingly in its first $j$ positions and whose row $i$ carries the remaining belt entries increasingly in its last $\rho_i-j+1$ positions. Among the tableaux $t^\rho\cdot d$, $d\in D$, exactly one fails to be standard, namely $g$, and every other one strictly dominates $g$: each of them agrees with $t^\rho$ outside the belt and is determined by the $j$-element subset $S$ of belt entries that it places increasingly in the first $j$ positions of row $i+1$, the complementary belt entries occupying increasingly the last $\rho_i-j+1$ positions of row $i$; column $j$ fails exactly when $\min(\mathrm{belt}\setminus S)>\max(S)$, that is, when $S$ consists of the $j$ smallest belt entries, which is $g$. For the dominance comparison, the cumulative counts $c_{m,k}$ of step 1.2 for $k\le i-1$ and $k\ge i+1$ do not depend on $S$; for $k=i$ row $i$ carries the belt complement of $S$, and $g$ carries the largest $\rho_i-j+1$ belt entries, whose count function is pointwise minimal, so every other belt tableau strictly dominates $g$.

**The straightening identity.** Let $
u$ be the partition obtained by sorting the parts of $\alpha$. Rewriting the left-hand side of the belt identity of step 2.3 as row-module basis elements through step 3.1, and applying step 2.2 to its right-hand side, the belt identity becomes $$x_ho T_{d(g)}=h-\sum_{d\in D,\ d
e d(g)}x_ho T_{d},$$ where $h$ is an $R$-linear combination of elements $T_{d_
u(s')}^*x_
u T_{d_
u(t')}$ with $s',t'$ row standard, and the tableaux $t^ho\cdot d$ with $d\in D$, $d
e d(g)$, are all standard and strictly more dominant than $g$; here $
u$ is strictly greater than $ho$ in lexicographic order because the part $ho_i+1$ exceeds $ho_i$ while all earlier parts are retained and sorting can only move such an increase earlier.

**Two-index straightening.** Every $m^\rho_{st}$ with $s,t$ row standard and $t$ non-standard is an $R$-linear combination of elements $m^{\rho_0}_{uv}$ with either $\rho_0\rhd_{\mathrm{lex}}\rho$, or $\rho_0=\rho$ and $u\unrhd s$, $v\rhd t$. Indeed, writing $t=g\cdot w$ with $\ell(d(t))=\ell(d(g))+\ell(w)$ at an offending Garnir node (every non-standard row-standard tableau arises this way: choose a column violation, order the forced upper-tail/lower-prefix inversions canonically, and reach the Garnir tableau by adjacent swaps of incomparable entries, reversing the process to obtain $w$), multiply the identity of step 4.1 on the left by $T_{d(s)}^*$ and on the right by $T_w$; step 2.1 pushes every same-shape term strictly above $t$ while the higher-shape terms are handled by descending lexicographic induction, the left index is treated symmetrically using $m^\rho_{st}=m^\rho_{ts}{}^*$, and the finite dominance order on row-standard tableaux makes the inner induction terminate. Composing with step 2.2, every $m^\alpha_{st}$ with $\alpha$ a composition is a combination of partition-indexed $m^\nu_{uv}$ with $u,v$ standard.

**The Murphy basis.** For $\alpha=(1^n)$ one has $x_{(1^n)}=1$, so every standard basis element is a Murphy element and the standard Murphy family spans $H$ by step 5.1. Its cardinality is $\sum_\rho(f^\rho)^2=n!$ by [F3], equal to the rank of the free module $H$, so writing the family in the standard basis gives a square matrix that, having a right inverse, has unit determinant; hence the family including the empty shape is an $R$-basis of $H$, and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$ follows from $x_\rho^*=x_\rho$ and [F1]. This is clause (1).

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

For every $n\ge0$,
$$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}(f^\lambda)^2=n!,$$
where $f^\lambda$ is the number of standard $\lambda$-tableaux and
$f^\varnothing=1$, $0!=1$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$\alpha,\nu\vdash n$ be partitions of $n$ with conjugate $\nu'$ and
$x_\alpha,y_\nu\in H_{R,q}(S_n)$ as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]. If $\alpha$
is not dominated by $\nu'$ in the sense of
[[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]], that is, if
$\sum_{i\le k}\alpha_i>\sum_{i\le k}\nu'_i$ for some $k\ge1$, then
$$x_\alpha Hy_\nu=0.$$
The vanishing is a universal Laurent-polynomial identity, remains valid at
singular parameters and uses no cancellation of $q+1$. The proof explicitly
sorts parabolic double cosets and uses the zero product
$(1+T_i)(1-q^{-1}T_i)=0$. Empty shapes and $n=0,1$ are included. No choice
principle is used.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

For all partitions $\lambda$ and $\mu$ of the same integer $n$,
$$\lambda\unrhd\mu\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\mu'\unrhd\lambda'.$$

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$

for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining

$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

derivations.claim: **The order on row-standard tableaux.** For an $\alpha$-tableau $u$ and integers $m\ge0$, $k\ge1$ put $c_{m,k}(u):=\#\{x\in B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_k:u(x)\le m\}$, where $B_1,B_2,\dots$ are the row blocks of the shape, and write $u\le v$ when $c_{m,k}(u)\le c_{m,k}(v)$ for all $m,k$. Swapping the labels $i$ and $i+1$ changes only the counts at $m=i$, and $c_{i,k}(u\cdot s_i)=c_{i-1,k}(u)+[\,i+1$ lies in the first $k$ blocks of $u\,]$, because the label $i$ is replaced by $i+1$ and every other label $\le i$ stays put. Hence for row-standard $u,v$ the relations $u\le v$ and $v\le u$ hold simultaneously only when $u=v$: the numbers $c_{m,k}$ record the multiset of labels in each row block, and a row-standard tableau is its row multisets sorted increasingly. Moreover, interchanging the entries of two incomparable cells of a standard tableau again has increasing rows and columns, because every comparable pair involving either of the two cells keeps its relative order.

**Ascending standard chains and their local shape.** Let $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)$, $t\ne t^\mu$, and put $d:=d_\mu(t)\ne1$. Since $d$ is not the identity there is an index $i$ with $d(i)>d(i+1)$; such an index is a right descent, so $\ell(ds_i)=\ell(d)-1$. In the row-reading word of $t$ the value $i$ occurs at position $d(i)$ and the value $i+1$ at the earlier position $d(i+1)$. The two cells are incomparable: the cell of $i+1$ is not northwest of the cell of $i$, since in a standard tableau a northwest cell carries the smaller value, and it is not southeast either, since a southeast cell is later in row-reading order. Therefore $t\cdot s_i$ is standard and $d_\mu(t\cdot s_i)=ds_i$. Iterating gives a descending chain from $t$ to $t^\mu$ in which each step is a standard adjacent swap of incomparable cells and decreases $\ell(d_\mu(\cdot))$ by one; reversing it gives an ascending chain $t_0=t^\mu,t_1,\dots,t_r=t$ of standard $\mu$-tableaux with $t_{j+1}=t_j\cdot s_{i_j}$ and $\ell(d_\mu(t_{j+1}))=\ell(d_\mu(t_j))+1$. In such a step the value $i:=i_j$ precedes the value $i+1$ in the row-reading order of $t_j$, so the two cells are distinct and lie in different rows, with the row of $i$ strictly above the row of $i+1$; the cell of $i$ also lies in a strictly later column than the cell of $i+1$, since otherwise the cell in the row of $i$ and the column of $i+1$ would carry an integer strictly between $i$ and $i+1$. Transposing, the standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s_j:=t_j'$ satisfy $s_{j+1}=s_j\cdot s_i$, the value $i$ lies in a row strictly below the row of $i+1$ in $s_j$, and $\ell(d_\lambda(s_j)s_i)=\ell(d_\lambda(s_j))-1$.

**Base case of the triangular expansion.** Let $u\in S_\mu$. The group $S_\mu$ permutes the intervals $B_j=\{\lambda'_1+\cdots+\lambda'_{j-1}+1,\dots,\lambda'_1+\cdots+\lambda'_j\}$, and these are exactly the label sets of the columns of $t_\lambda$; they are intervals, increasing in $j$. For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest

derivations.claim: **The $\theta$-image of the Murphy basis.** Since $\theta$ is an $R$-algebra automorphism of $H$ and $\{m^\mu_{st}\}$ is an $R$-basis by [F2], the family $\{\theta(m^\mu_{st})\}$ is again an $R$-basis, and $\theta(m_{st})=\theta(T_{d(s)}^*)\theta(x_\lambda)\theta(T_{d(t)})$ by multiplicativity, with $\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda$ by [F1]; also $\theta(m_{st})^*=\theta(m_{st}^*)=\theta(m_{ts})$ because $\theta$ commutes with $*$.

**The transported ideals and cellular structure.** For a partition $\rho$, the ideal $I^{\unrhd\rho}$ is spanned by the $m^\mu_{uv}$ with $\mu\unrhd\rho$ by [F3], so its image $\theta(I^{\unrhd\rho})$ is spanned by the corresponding $\theta(m^\mu_{uv})$; as the image of a two-sided ideal under an automorphism it is a two-sided ideal, and likewise for $\theta(I^{\rhd\rho})$. Moreover $\theta(I^{\unrhd\rho})\subseteq\theta(I^{\unrhd\rho'})$ whenever $\rho\unrhd\rho'$, and the transported cell law holds: for $h\in H$, $\theta(m_{st})\theta(h)=\theta(m_{st}h)\equiv\sum_v r_v\theta(m_{sv})\pmod{\theta(I^{\rhd\rho})}$ with the same coefficients $r_v$ as in [F2], independent of the first index. Hence $(\{\theta(m_{st})\},\unrhd)$ is a cellular basis with the same dominance poset and the $\theta$-image filtration.

**The ideal subspaces move.** Take $n=2$ and $\lambda=(2)$. Here $x_{(2)}=1+T_1$ spans $I^{\unrhd(2)}=R(1+T_1)$ (the only Murphy shape dominating $(2)$ is $(2)$ itself, with a single standard tableau), while $\theta(x_{(2)})=1+\theta(T_1)=1+(q-1)-T_1=q-T_1$. A relation $q-T_1=c(1+T_1)$ with $c\in R$ would compare the coefficients of $1$ and of $T_1$ in the standard basis and force $c=q$ and $c=-1$, hence $q=-1$, which fails for a general unit $q$; therefore $\theta(I^{\unrhd(2)})\ne I^{\unrhd(2)}$. By step 1.2 both are two-sided ideals with the same shape index, so the poset is preserved but the ideal subspaces are not.

**The module isomorphism.** Put $K:=M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$, so that $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/K$ by [F2]. The assignment $m+K\mapsto\theta(m)+\theta(K)$ on representatives $m\in M(\lambda)$ is well defined and bijective, since $\theta$ is a bijection carrying $K$ onto $\theta(M(\lambda))\cap\theta(I^{\rhd\lambda})$; it is $H$-linear because for $m\in M(\lambda)$ and $h\in H$ one has $\theta(m\theta(h))=\theta(m)\theta^2(h)=\theta(m)h$ using $\theta^2=\mathrm{id}$ by [F1]. Its target is by construction the quotient of the transported row by the transported higher ideal, i.e. the cell module of the transported basis of step 1.2. Hence $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$ (the same underlying module with action $m\cdot h=m\theta(h)$) is isomorphic to that transported cell row, is free of rank $f^\lambda$ with basis $\{\theta(m_t)\}$ and satisfies the transported cell law.

**The transported form.** Define $G_\lambda^\theta$ on the underlying module of $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$ by $G_\lambda^\theta(x,y):=G_\lambda(x,y)$. Symmetry is immediate from [F2], and associativity for the twisted action follows from the ordinary associativity: $G_\lambda^\theta(x\cdot h,y)=G_\lambda(x\theta(h),y)=G_\lambda(x,y\theta(h)^*)=G_\lambda(x,y\theta(h^*))=G_\lambda^\theta(x,y\cdot h^*)$, using that $\theta$ commutes with $*$ and $\theta^2=\mathrm{id}$ by [F1]. Its radical is $\{x:G_\lambda(x,y)=0\ \forall y\}=\operatorname{rad}G_\lambda$, which is a submodule for the twisted action as well. Under the identification $x\mapsto\theta(x)$ of step 2.2 the form becomes $G_\lambda^\theta(\theta u,\theta v)=G_\lambda(u,v)$ for $u,v\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, which is exactly the Murphy form of the transported basis, because multiplying two transported basis elements gives $\theta(m_{us})\theta(m_{tv})=\theta(m_{us}m_{tv})\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)\theta(m_{uv})\pmod{\theta(I^{\rhd\lambda})}$ by [F2]; thus $G_\lambda^\theta$ is the transported form of clause 3 and $x\mapsto\theta(x)$ is an isometry.

**Base change and the conjugate clause.** Every element, ideal, quotient and form above is defined by formulas with coefficients in $\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$ and the identities are identities of such formulas, so they specialize along any ring map $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$, by [F4]; in particular the transported basis stays a basis and the cell law and form identities are preserved. Applying clauses 1-3 to the conjugate partition $\lambda'$, which satisfies $f^{\lambda'}=f^\lambda$ by [F2], gives clause 4. Only the presentation of $H$, the automorphism $\theta$, the Murphy cellular structure and its form are used, so no choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$, the permutation form $\beta$ on
$M(\lambda)$ is well defined, symmetric and $R$-bilinear, with
$\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}$ on the
distinguished basis of
[[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]. It is
$H$-contravariant:
$$\beta(xh,y)=\beta(x,yh^*)\qquad(x,y\in M(\lambda),\ h\in H).$$
Its restriction $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ to the polytabloid module $P(\lambda)$
satisfies the same identity for $x,y\in P(\lambda)$ and is called the DJ form.
Both $\beta$ and $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $\lambda\vdash n$
with conjugate $\mu=\lambda'$, and let $H$, $M(\lambda)=x_\lambda H$,
$P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with $z_\lambda=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_\mu$, the
permutation form $\beta$ and the DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ be as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]. Write
$b_r:=x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(r)}$ for the row-standard $\lambda$-tableaux $r$
(the distinguished basis of $M(\lambda)$) and
$$e_t:=z_\lambda T_{d_\mu(t)}\in P(\lambda)\qquad(t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)).$$
For row-standard $\lambda$-tableaux $u,v$ write $u\le v$ when for all
$m,k\ge1$ the first $k$ rows of $u$ contain at most as many labels $\le m$ as
the first $k$ rows of $v$, and let $t'$ be the transpose of $t$, a standard
$\lambda$-tableau. Then:

1. $\{e_t:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is an $R$-basis of $P(\lambda)$, so
   $P(\lambda)$ is free of rank $f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$, and
   the inclusion $P(\lambda)\subseteq M(\lambda)$ splits as a map of
   $R$-modules.

2. For every $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)$ one has, with coefficients
   $a_{r,t}\in R$,
   $$e_t=q^{\ell(d_\mu(t))}\,b_{t'}+\sum_{r<t'}a_{r,t}\,b_r,$$
   where the sum runs over the row-standard $r$ with $r\le t'$, $r\ne t'$; the
   square minor with rows $\{t':t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is therefore
   triangular with respect to any linear extension of the order $\le$ on
   $\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$, with diagonal entries
   $q^{\ell(d_\mu(t))}$, all units of $R$.

3. The Gram matrix of the DJ form in the basis $\{e_t\}$ is
   $$B_{tu}=\sum_{r}a_{r,t}a_{r,u}q^{\ell(d_\lambda(r))}\qquad(t,u\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)),$$
   with $a_{r,t}$ as in clause 2. Unit triangularity is a property of the
   embedding, not of the Gram matrix: $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ may be degenerate.

4. Let $(i,j)$ be a Garnir node of $\mu$, that is, a node of $\mu$ with
   $j\le\mu_{i+1}$, put
   $\alpha=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_{i-1},j-1,\mu_i+1,\mu_{i+1}-j,\mu_{i+2},\dots)$
   with zero parts deleted and $D:=S_\alpha\cap D_\mu$, and let
   $\theta(T_d)\in H$ be the product of the elements
   $\theta(T_r)=(q-1)-T_r$ over a reduced word of $d$
   ([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Then
   $$z_\lambda\sum_{d\in D}\theta(T_d)=0\qquad\text{in }P(\lambda).$$
   The coefficients are determined by the finite coset identity of step 4.1 and
   survive every base change; together with the unit minor of clause 2 these
   relations give a finite straightening of the elements $z_\lambda T_w$ to
   the standard basis $\{e_t\}$.

5. Every clause is compatible with the base change
   $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$. The proof
   uses no generic semisimplicity, divides by no quantum factorial and uses no
   choice principle.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$\alpha,\nu\vdash n$ be partitions of $n$ with conjugate $\nu'$ and
$x_\alpha,y_\nu\in H_{R,q}(S_n)$ as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]. If $\alpha$
is not dominated by $\nu'$ in the sense of
[[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]], that is, if
$\sum_{i\le k}\alpha_i>\sum_{i\le k}\nu'_i$ for some $k\ge1$, then
$$x_\alpha Hy_\nu=0.$$
The vanishing is a universal Laurent-polynomial identity, remains valid at
singular parameters and uses no cancellation of $q+1$. The proof explicitly
sorts parabolic double cosets and uses the zero product
$(1+T_i)(1-q^{-1}T_i)=0$. Empty shapes and $n=0,1$ are included. No choice
principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism

**The adjoint is an isomorphism.** The adjoint map $\Phi\colon C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$, $c\mapsto B_\lambda(c,-)$, is a well-defined $H$-module homomorphism by the balancing of step 2.1 and [F5]. It is surjective: the map $M(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$, $a\mapsto\beta(a,-)$, is the composition of the inverse of the isomorphism $M(\lambda)\to M(\lambda)^\circ$, $a\mapsto\beta(a,-)$ (its matrix in the basis $\{b_r\}$ and its dual basis is diagonal with the unit entries $q^{\ell(d_\lambda(r))}$), with the restriction $M(\lambda)^\circ\to P(\lambda)^\circ$, which is surjective because $P(\lambda)$ is a split submodule of $M(\lambda)$ by [F2]; since $K$ is killed by step 2.1, this surjection factors through the quotient $M(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, so $\Phi$ is surjective. A surjection between free modules of the same finite rank has a right inverse: choose preimages of the finitely many basis vectors, whose coordinate columns form a right inverse of the square matrix of $\Phi$; hence $\det\Phi$ is a unit of $R$ and $\Phi$ is an isomorphism. $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.
