Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $\lambda\vdash n$
with conjugate $\mu=\lambda'$, and let $H$, $M(\lambda)=x_\lambda H$,
$P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with $z_\lambda=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_\mu$, the
permutation form $\beta$ and the DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ be as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]. Write
$b_r:=x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(r)}$ for the row-standard $\lambda$-tableaux $r$
(the distinguished basis of $M(\lambda)$) and
$$e_t:=z_\lambda T_{d_\mu(t)}\in P(\lambda)\qquad(t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)).$$
For row-standard $\lambda$-tableaux $u,v$ write $u\le v$ when for all
$m,k\ge1$ the first $k$ rows of $u$ contain at most as many labels $\le m$ as
the first $k$ rows of $v$, and let $t'$ be the transpose of $t$, a standard
$\lambda$-tableau. Then:

1. $\{e_t:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is an $R$-basis of $P(\lambda)$, so
   $P(\lambda)$ is free of rank $f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$, and
   the inclusion $P(\lambda)\subseteq M(\lambda)$ splits as a map of
   $R$-modules.

2. For every $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)$ one has, with coefficients
   $a_{r,t}\in R$,
   $$e_t=q^{\ell(d_\mu(t))}\,b_{t'}+\sum_{r<t'}a_{r,t}\,b_r,$$
   where the sum runs over the row-standard $r$ with $r\le t'$, $r\ne t'$; the
   square minor with rows $\{t':t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is therefore
   triangular with respect to any linear extension of the order $\le$ on
   $\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$, with diagonal entries
   $q^{\ell(d_\mu(t))}$, all units of $R$.

3. The Gram matrix of the DJ form in the basis $\{e_t\}$ is
   $$B_{tu}=\sum_{r}a_{r,t}a_{r,u}q^{\ell(d_\lambda(r))}\qquad(t,u\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)),$$
   with $a_{r,t}$ as in clause 2. Unit triangularity is a property of the
   embedding, not of the Gram matrix: $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ may be degenerate.

4. Let $(i,j)$ be a Garnir node of $\mu$, that is, a node of $\mu$ with
   $j\le\mu_{i+1}$, put
   $\alpha=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_{i-1},j-1,\mu_i+1,\mu_{i+1}-j,\mu_{i+2},\dots)$
   with zero parts deleted and $D:=S_\alpha\cap D_\mu$, and let
   $\theta(T_d)\in H$ be the product of the elements
   $\theta(T_r)=(q-1)-T_r$ over a reduced word of $d$
   ([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Then
   $$z_\lambda\sum_{d\in D}\theta(T_d)=0\qquad\text{in }P(\lambda).$$
   The coefficients are determined by the finite coset identity of step 4.1 and
   survive every base change; together with the unit minor of clause 2 these
   relations give a finite straightening of the elements $z_\lambda T_w$ to
   the standard basis $\{e_t\}$.

5. Every clause is compatible with the base change
   $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$. The proof
   uses no generic semisimplicity, divides by no quantum factorial and uses no
   choice principle.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$, the permutation form $\beta$ on
$M(\lambda)$ is well defined, symmetric and $R$-bilinear, with
$\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}$ on the
distinguished basis of
[[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]. It is
$H$-contravariant:
$$\beta(xh,y)=\beta(x,yh^*)\qquad(x,y\in M(\lambda),\ h\in H).$$
Its restriction $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ to the polytabloid module $P(\lambda)$
satisfies the same identity for $x,y\in P(\lambda)$ and is called the DJ form.
Both $\beta$ and $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$. No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$, $\lambda\vdash n$, and let
$\theta$ be the involutive automorphism of
[[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. Let $m_{st}$, the ideals
$I^{\unrhd\lambda}$, $I^{\rhd\lambda}$, the cell module
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, its basis classes $m_t$ and the Murphy form
$G_\lambda$ be as in
[[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]. Then:

1. For standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$ one has
   $\theta(m_{st})=\theta(T_{d(s)}^*)\,\theta(m_\lambda)\,\theta(T_{d(t)})$
   with $\theta(m_\lambda)=\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda$;
   the family $\{\theta(m^\mu_{st}):\mu\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$
   is again an $R$-basis of $H$; the spans $\theta(I^{\unrhd\lambda})$ and
   $\theta(I^{\rhd\lambda})$ of the $\theta$-images of the corresponding basis
   elements are two-sided ideals of $H$, and the transported family is again a
   cellular basis with the same dominance poset, whose ideal filtration is the
   $\theta$-image of the original one. The image ideals are in general
   *different* subspaces from the originals: already for $n=2$ and
   $\lambda=(2)$ one has $\theta(x_{(2)})=q-T_1\notin R(1+T_1)=I^{\unrhd(2)}$.
   The poset is preserved; the ideal subspaces are not, in general.

2. The assignment $m\mapsto\theta(m)$ on representatives is a well-defined
   isomorphism of right $H$-modules
   $$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta\longrightarrow \theta(M(\lambda))/\bigl(\theta(M(\lambda))\cap\theta(I^{\rhd\lambda})\bigr),$$
   whose target is the cell module of the transported basis; in particular
   $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$ is free of rank $f^\lambda$ with basis
   $\{\theta(m_t):t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ and satisfies the
   transported cell law with the same coefficients.

3. The transported form $G_\lambda^\theta$, defined on the transported basis
   by $G_\lambda^\theta(\theta x,\theta y):=G_\lambda(x,y)$ for
   $x,y\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, i.e. read on the underlying module of
   $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$ by $G_\lambda^\theta(x,y)=G_\lambda(x,y)$,
   is symmetric, is associative for the twisted action in the sense
   $G_\lambda^\theta(x\cdot h,y)=G_\lambda^\theta(x,y\cdot h^*)$, and has the
   same radical as $G_\lambda$; the map $x\mapsto\theta(x)$ is an isometry from
   the twisted cell module onto the cell module of the transported basis. All
   identities specialize under every base change.

4. In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ is free of rank
   $f^{\lambda'}=f^\lambda$ and carries the transported form
   $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$. No choice principle is used.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field and let $J=J(A)$. Then
$J$ is nilpotent, and the quotient algebra $A/J$ is semisimple.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with its basis $\{m_t\}$, $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$,
the permutation form $\beta$ on $M(\lambda)$ and the DJ form on $P(\lambda)$
be as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]],
[[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and
[[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]. Then:

1. Setting $B_\lambda(m_s,p):=\beta(x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(s)},p)$ for
   $s\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$ and $p\in P(\lambda)$ defines an explicit
   $R$-bilinear pairing
   $B_\lambda\colon C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\times P(\lambda)\to R$ that is
   $H$-balanced, $B_\lambda(mh,p)=B_\lambda(m,ph^*)$, and whose adjoint
   $c\mapsto B_\lambda(c,-)$ is an isomorphism of right $H$-modules
   $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$ onto the star-contragredient
   module of [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. No
   nondegeneracy of the DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ is required.

2. Equivalently, the kernel of the quotient map
   $M(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is the orthogonal complement
   $P(\lambda)^\perp=\{a\in M(\lambda):\beta(a,p)=0\text{ for all }p\in P(\lambda)\}$,
   and its preimage under the quotient is
   $M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$; the pairing matrices in the bases
   $\{m_s\}$ and $\{e_t\}$ have entries $B_\lambda(m_s,e_t)=q^{\ell(d_\lambda(s))}a_{t,d_\lambda(s)}$
   and determinant a unit of $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$.

3. All statements are compatible with every base change $A\to R$,
   $v\mapsto q$; the construction uses no generic semisimplicity, no
   nondegeneracy of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ and no choice principle.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: **The comparison map.** By [F2] the map $F\colon C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta\to P(\lambda)$, $F(m):=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(m)$, is a well-defined surjective $H$-module map. Both sides are free of finite rank $f^{\lambda'}=f^\lambda$ by [F2] and [F4], so choosing preimages of the basis $\{e_t\}$ gives a right inverse of the square matrix of $F$; its determinant is a unit of $R$ and $F$ is an isomorphism. Put $\Phi_\lambda:=F^{-1}$. Then $\Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0$ and $\Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)$ for all $h\in H$, since $F(m_0\theta(h))=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(m_0\theta(h))=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(m_0)h=z_\lambda h$; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$, and $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(m)$.

**Generic semisimplicity and proportionality.** Work first over the Laurent domain $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ and its fraction field $K=\mathbb Q(q)$. The regular trace form $(a,b)\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}(L_{ab})$ on $H_K=K\otimes_AH_v(n)$ has Gram matrix in the standard basis $\{\operatorname{Tr}(T_uT_v)\}_{u,v}$; its determinant is a Laurent polynomial whose value at $q=1$ is the determinant of $n!$ times the permutation matrix $u\leftrightarrow u^{-1}$ in the group algebra $\mathbb Q[S_n]$, hence nonzero. Therefore the regular trace form is nondegenerate over $K$; since $L_{ab}$ is nilpotent for $a\in J(H_K)$ and every $b$, every such trace vanishes, so $J(H_K)=0$ and $H_K$ is semisimple by [F6]. In the semisimple algebra $H_K$ the layer $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\otimes C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with multiplication $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=G_{\lambda'}(b,c)a\otimes d$ is a nonzero subquotient of $H_K$, hence semisimple; if $G_{\lambda'}$ were degenerate over $K$, then $(\operatorname{rad}G_{\lambda'})\otimes C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ would be a nonzero square-zero two-sided ideal of that layer, which is impossible in a semisimple algebra. Thus $G_{\lambda'}$ is nondegenerate over $K$, the same layer identification $C\otimes C\cong\operatorname{End}_K(C)$ shows that $C=C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')_K$ is a simple $H_K$-module, and $\operatorname{End}_{H_K}(C)=K$ by Schur. Consequently two $H_K$-contravariant $K$-bilinear forms on $C$, one of them nonzero, are proportional: if $G_1=G_{\lambda'}$ is the nonzero one and $G_2$ is any other, the relation $G_1(ux,y)=G_2(x,y)$ defines $u\in\operatorname{End}_K(C)$, and contravariance of both forms gives $G_1(u(xh)-u(x)h,y)=0$ for all $x,h,y$, so $u\in\operatorname{End}_{H_K}(C)=K$ and $G_2=uG_1$.

**The two values at the generator.** By [F2] one has $z_\lambda=\sum_{u\in S_{\lambda'}}(-q)^{-\ell(u)}b_{t_\lambda\cdot u}$, the elements $t_\lambda\cdot u$ are row standard, and $\ell(d_\lambda(t_\lambda\cdot u))=\ell(w_\lambda u)=L+\ell(u)$. Hence by [F3] $\beta(z_\lambda,z_\lambda)=\sum_uq^{-2\ell(u)}q^{L+\ell(u)}=q^L\sum_uq^{-\ell(u)}=q^{L-N}P_{\lambda'}(q)$, using $u\mapsto w_0(S_{\lambda'})u$ for the last equality and [F4] for $G_{\lambda'}(m_0,m_0)=P_{\lambda'}(q)$. So with $u_\lambda(q):=q^{N-L}$ one has $G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda z_\lambda,\Phi_\lambda z_\lambda)=G_{\lambda'}(m_0,m_0)=P_{\lambda'}(q)=q^{N-L}\beta(z_\lambda,z_\lambda)=u_\lambda(q)\beta_{P(\lambda)}(z_\lambda,z_\lambda)$ by [F5].

**The form identity, radicals and the conjugate chain.** The pullback of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ along $\Phi_\lambda$ is an $H_K$-contravariant form on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')_K$, and so is $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ by [F5]; the latter is nonzero because $G_{\lambda'}^\theta(m_0,m_0)=P_{\lambda'}(q)\ne0$. By step 1.2 they are proportional, say $G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=\lambda\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)$; evaluating at $x=y=z_\lambda$ and dividing by the nonzero element $P_{\lambda'}(q)$ in the field $K$ gives $\lambda=u_\lambda(q)=q^{N-L}$ by step 2.1. Both sides of the identity have entries in $A$, and $A\to K$ is injective, so the identity holds in $A$ and, by [F8], after every base change to $R$. Since $\Phi_\lambda$ is an isomorphism and $u_\lambda$ is a unit, $\Phi_\lambda$ carries the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$; passing to the quotients gives $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the case of a zero quotient, and over a PID the submodules defined by the divisibility of the form values correspond because the identifying isomorphism scales the forms by a unit. Applying the identity with $\lambda$ replaced by $\lambda'$ gives $P(\lambda')\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$, and combining with [F7] and $(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$ from [F1] yields $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$. For $\lambda=\varnothing$ one has $L=N=0$, $\Phi_\lambda$ is the identity of the free rank-one module and $u_\lambda=1$. Only the presentation of $H$, the trace form, Jacobson nilpotence, the cellular structure of $H_K$, the trace pairing and the annihilation were used; no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: The formulas of steps 1.1-2.2 are uniform in lambda with n>=0 and include n=0: for lambda=emptyset, P(emptyset)=F is the trivial module, D^emptyset its head, and the multiplicity statement reads 1=1; step 3.1's zero case includes it.

Clause 3 includes the zero case, repeated in step 3.1; the multiplicity statement of step 2.2 is vacuous for zero modules and the proof divides by nothing, all structure constants becoming integers at q=1 by step 1.1.
n=1: there is a single partition, P((1)) and C_M((1)) are the trivial rank-one modules with the same head, and the dictionary of steps 2.1-2.2 is the identity statement.

Extreme shapes: at lambda=(n) or (1^n) the modules P and C_M have rank one and the multiplicity formulas of step 2.2 reduce to the trivial simple modules; the identifications of step 1.1 include these shapes.

The two ends of the dictionary are the specialization q=1 of step 1.1, with the explicit tabloid and polytabloid identifications, and the generic unit q in F^x of step 2.2's exact twist, with the conditional Schur dictionary of step 3.1 applied at the cases it names.
The Statement records that no choice principle is used; all maps in steps 1.1-3.1 are canonical twist and exactness identifications.

boundaries.reason: Clause 3 is explicitly conditional, supposing a corner already proved to send W(lambda) to C_M(lambda) and L(lambda) to D^lambda_M; the conditional is proved in step 3.1 and no unconditioned equivalence is claimed.
No converse is claimed; the corollary does not assert the untwisted conjugate-duality statement and step 3.1 says the untwisted identity is a different formula.

citations.quote:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write
$\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let
$P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign
automorphism $\theta$ be as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]],
[[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and
[[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of
[[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules
   $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$
   where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and
   the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$
   and read in the twist; in particular
   $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for
   $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. Moreover
   $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(m)$.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of
   [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and
   $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$,
   $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$
   over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no
   potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit
   $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto
   the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients
   is an isomorphism, and the DJ head corresponds to the twisted Murphy head,
   $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$,
   including the zero-quotient case. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the
   unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their
   reductions. One also obtains
   $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the
   dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign
   transport. No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $n\ge0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $\Omega_\lambda$ be the finite set
of $\lambda$-tabloids; for a $\lambda$-tableau $t$ write $\{t\}$ for its
tabloid ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]). The
**integral tabloid module** is the free abelian group on $\Omega_\lambda$,

$$M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}:=\mathbb Z^{(\Omega_\lambda)} =\Bigl\{\sum_{T\in\Omega_\lambda}a_T\,T:\ a_T\in\mathbb Z,\ \text{only finitely many }a_T\ne0\Bigr\},$$

with the tabloids as standard $\mathbb Z$-basis
([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). The left action of $S_n$ on
tabloids extends $\mathbb Z$-linearly to $M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, so that
$M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ is a $\mathbb Z[S_n]$-module. For every $\lambda$-tableau
$t$ put

$$\kappa_t:=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma \in\mathbb Z[S_n],\qquad e_t:=\kappa_t\cdot\{t\}=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\, \{\gamma\cdot t\}\in M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},$$

the **integral column polytabloid**; every coefficient lies in
$\{0,1,-1\}$ ([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]).
The **integral Specht lattice** is the $\mathbb Z[S_n]$-submodule

$$S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}:=\text{the }\mathbb Z\text{-span of } \{\,e_s:\ s\text{ a }\lambda\text{-tableau}\,\}\subseteq M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}.$$

For a commutative ring $R$ let $M^\lambda_R:=R^{(\Omega_\lambda)}$ be the free
$R$-module on the tabloids and let $S^\lambda_R\subseteq M^\lambda_R$ be the
$R$-span of the polytabloids $\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)
\{\gamma\cdot t\}$, $t$ a $\lambda$-tableau. The **standard polytabloids** are
the $e_s$ with $s$ a standard $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]).

This item records three facts. First, the standard polytabloids form a
$\mathbb Z$-basis of $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, so the integral Specht lattice has
explicit finite rank. Second, for every commutative ring $R$ the canonical map
$R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\to R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}
M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\cong M^\lambda_R$ is injective onto $S^\lambda_R$: the
lattice is a direct summand of the free tabloid module and is compatible with
base change, including rings of prime characteristic. Third, for
$\lambda=\varnothing$ the module has rank one and is generated by the empty
polytabloid.

Let $F$ be a field, $n\ge0$, $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $\lambda'$ be the
conjugate partition. Write $\Omega_\lambda$ for the finite set of
$\lambda$-tabloids and let
$$M^\lambda_F=F^{(\Omega_\lambda)},\qquad S^\lambda_F\subseteq M^\lambda_F,\qquad \kappa_t=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma,\qquad e_t=\kappa_t\{t\}$$
be the field-valued tabloid module, the span of the polytabloids inside it,
the column antisymmetrizer, and the polytabloid of a $\lambda$-tableau $t$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). Let
$$\beta_F:M^\lambda_F\times M^\lambda_F\longrightarrow F$$
be the $F$-bilinear form for which the tabloid basis is orthonormal
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]]), and for a
subspace $V\subseteq M^\lambda_F$ put
$$V^\perp:=\{x\in M^\lambda_F:\beta_F(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\}.$$

Let $\operatorname{sgn}$ be the sign representation of $S_n$ on the line
$F w$, so that $\sigma\cdot w=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)w$
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]]), and let
$$S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$$
be the tensor product of $F[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w):=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, a
finite-dimensional $F[S_n]$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]). For a
finite-dimensional $F[S_n]$-module $D$ the **dual** is
$D^*=\operatorname{Hom}_F(D,F)$ with $(\sigma\cdot f)(v):=f(\sigma^{-1}v)$.

Fix the **row-filled** $\lambda$-tableau $t_0$, whose $i$-th row carries the
block $B_i=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\dots,\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$
in increasing order, and let $t_0^{\mathsf T}$ be its transpose, a
$\lambda'$-tableau. For a $\lambda'$-tableau $u$ let $\sigma_u\in S_n$ be the
unique permutation with $\sigma_u\cdot t_0^{\mathsf T}=u$, and let
$u^{\mathsf T}$ be the transpose of $u$, a $\lambda$-tableau. Define an
$F$-linear map on the tabloid basis of $M^{\lambda'}_F$ by
$$\theta(\{u\}):=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma_u)\,\bigl(e_{u^{\mathsf T}}\otimes w\bigr) \ \in\ S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$

**Lemma.** With this notation:

1. $\theta$ does not depend on the chosen representative $u$ of the tabloid
   $\{u\}$; it is a well-defined $F[S_n]$-module homomorphism
   $\theta:M^{\lambda'}_F\to S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ with
   $\theta(\{t_0^{\mathsf T}\})=e_{t_0}\otimes w$.
2. $\theta$ is surjective and
   $\ker\theta=(S^{\lambda'}_F)^\perp$.
3. Consequently $\theta$ induces $F[S_n]$-isomorphisms
   $$M^{\lambda'}_F/(S^{\lambda'}_F)^\perp\cong S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}, \qquad\text{hence}\qquad S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}\cong (S^{\lambda'}_F)^*,$$
   the second being the composite with $x\mapsto\beta_F(x,\cdot)|_{S^{\lambda'}_F}$.

No nondegeneracy of $\beta_F$ restricted to $S^{\lambda'}_F$ is assumed, and
the statement includes every prime characteristic, the case $n=0$, and the
case $F=\mathbb Q$ used in step 2.2. No step divides by a group order, none
uses positivity or averaging, and none uses characteristic zero beyond the
explicitly separated rational computation in steps 2.2 and 3.1.

Let $H_v(n)$ be the generic type-A Hecke algebra over
$A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ and let $q$ be a prime power. (1) The specialization
$v\mapsto1$ is an isomorphism of $\mathbb C$-algebras
$$\mathbb C\otimes_{A,\,v\mapsto1}H_v(n)\;\cong\;\mathbb C[S_n],$$
carrying $T_w$ to $w$; (2) the specialization $v\mapsto q$ is an isomorphism of
$\mathbb C$-algebras
$$\mathbb C\otimes_{A,\,v\mapsto q}H_v(n)\;\cong\;H=e_B\mathbb C[G]e_B,\qquad G=\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q),$$
carrying the generic generator $T_i$ to the standard basis element $T_{s_i}$;
(3) both specializations are semisimple $\mathbb C$-algebras, and the
isomorphisms are compatible with the standard bases ($\{T_w\}$ in each case).
No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: **The specialization at $q=1$.** At $q=1$ the algebra $H$ is the group algebra $F[S_n]$ by [F5], with $T_w=w$. The assignment $b_r=x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(r)}\mapsto\{t^\lambda\cdot d_\lambda(r)\}$ identifies the distinguished basis of $M(\lambda)$ with the tabloid basis of $M^\lambda_F$: the row group $S_\lambda$ acts on $t^\lambda$ by right multiplication with row-equivalent tabloids, and every tabloid is hit because $D_\lambda$ is a transversal. Under this identification $\beta$ becomes the standard orthonormal tabloid form, since every diagonal weight $q^{\ell(d_\lambda(r))}$ becomes $1$. Moreover $z_\lambda=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_{\lambda'}$ maps to the polytabloid of the column-filled tableau: $x_\lambda$ symmetrizes the rows, $w_\lambda$ carries $t^\lambda$ to $t_\lambda$, and $y_{\lambda'}=\sum_{u\in S_{\lambda'}}(-1)^{\ell(u)}T_u$ is the column antisymmetrizer of $t_\lambda$ at $q=1$ because $S_{\lambda'}$ is the column group of $\lambda$. Hence $e_t=z_\lambda T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)}$ maps to the polytabloid of the standard tableau obtained from $t_\lambda$ by the same permutation, and the family of these polytabloids is the standard basis of the image of $F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ in $F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ by [F3]. This gives the module and form part of clause 1 over every field; over $\mathbb Z$ the same computation gives the integral statement.

**The sign twist and the conjugate dictionary.** By [F2], at $q=1$ the automorphism $\theta$ is the pullback along $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$, so the twisted module $P(\lambda)^\theta$ is $P(\lambda)\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$; the isomorphism of [F1] therefore identifies $P(\lambda)\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ with the $\theta$-twist of $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$. The same-shape duality and the sign lemma identify the conjugate dual module $(S^{\lambda'}_F)^*$ with $S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F4], with the explicit tabloid map written there; since our $\theta$ is the same sign automorphism on $F[S_n]$, the two constructions agree, which is the compatibility asserted in clause 1.

**Multiplicities.** Let $q$ be a unit of a field and $\mu\vdash n$ with $D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}\ne0$. By [F1] the twist $\Phi_\lambda$ is an isomorphism $P(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$, and by [F2] twisting is exact and multiplies no composition multiplicity: for every simple right $H$-module $S$ one has $[P(\lambda):S]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta:S]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'):S^\theta]$. Applying the head identity of [F1] with $\lambda$ replaced by $\mu$ gives $D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, and applying $\theta$ gives $(D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta\cong D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}$. Substituting $S=D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ yields $[P(\lambda):D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'):D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]$, which is clause 2 together with the displayed identification of the simples.

**The conditional Schur dictionary and conclusion.** If a corner is already proved to send $W(\lambda)$ to $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ and $L(\lambda)$ to $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$, then applying it to $\lambda'$ gives $F(W(\lambda'))=C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and $F(L(\lambda'))=D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$. Tensoring the isomorphism of [F1] by $\theta$ gives $P(\lambda)^\theta\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$, and the head computation of step 2.2 gives $(D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta\cong D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$; hence $F(W(\lambda'))\cong P(\lambda)^\theta$ and $F(L(\lambda'))\cong(D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta$, including the zero case. This is a conditional application of the $\theta$-twisted identity and uses no Schur-algebra theorem as a prerequisite; the untwisted statement $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ without $\theta$ is a different formula. All constructions are exact and sign-free at the level of the group algebra, so no choice principle is used.

boundaries.reason: The counterexample is the fixed computation at n=3, q=1 over Q; no empty family or empty shape occurs, steps 1.1-2.1 evaluating only the two one-dimensional modules involved.

boundaries.evidence: The refutation turns on the scalars -1 and +1: step 1.2 computes m_0 T_i=-m_0 and step 1.1 computes T_i=+1, and the characteristic-zero cancellation of step 2.1, -f(m)=f(m) forcing f(m)=0, is legitimate over Q.
Both modules are one-dimensional by steps 1.1-1.2, P((3))=Q x_(3) and f^{(1^3)}=1, so the comparison is exactly the rank-one scalar comparison of step 2.1.

The degenerate configuration is the point of the example: lambda=(3) is the one-row extreme and lambda'=(1^3) the one-column extreme, q=1 makes the algebra the group algebra in step 1.1, and step 1.2 uses the Murphy elements 1+T_i=x_(2,1) of the higher shape.

boundaries.reason: There is no variable to take to a limit: the example is pinned at n=3, q=1, F=Q, and the only endpoint-type datum used is the inequality -1 not equal to 1 in characteristic zero in step 2.1.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement records that no choice principle is used; the computations of steps 1.1-2.1 are finite evaluations in the fixed group algebra Q[S_3].

boundaries.reason: The item refutes a claimed isomorphism rather than asserting a biconditional, so no implication direction is owed.
No converse is claimed; the twisted statement is recorded as consistent at the end of step 2.1 but its proof belongs to the comparison theorem.

$\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let
$P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign
automorphism $\theta$ be as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]],
[[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and
[[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of
[[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules
   $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$
   where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and
   the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$
   and read in the twist; in particular
   $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for

   [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and
   $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$,
   $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$
   over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no
   potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit
   $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

   the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients
   is an isomorphism, and the DJ head corresponds to the twisted Murphy head,
   $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$,
   including the zero-quotient case. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the
   unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their

derivations.claim: **The ordinary module is trivial.** At $q=1$ one has $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$ and $x_{(3)}T_i=\sum_wT_wT_i=\sum_wT_{ws_i}=x_{(3)}$ for each generator, because right multiplication by $s_i$ permutes the group and every $T_{ws_i}$ is again one of the summed basis elements; with the scalar carried along this reads $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}=x_{(3)}$ at $q=1$, and $P((3))=x_{(3)}H=\mathbb Q\,x_{(3)}$ is one-dimensional. Its dual is therefore also one-dimensional with trivial action.

**The cell is sign.** At $q=1$ the element $1+T_i$ lies in the higher ideal $I^{\rhd(1^3)}$, because $1+T_1$ and $1+T_2$ are the Murphy elements $x_{(2,1)}$ of shape $(2,1)\rhd(1^3)$ and $I^{\rhd(1^3)}$ is the span of all Murphy elements of shapes $\rhd(1^3)$; hence in the one-dimensional cell $m_0(1+T_i)=0$, that is, $m_0T_i=-m_0$. The cell form value is $1$, and the module is the sign module.

**No untwisted isomorphism.** A right $H$-module isomorphism $f\colon C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))\to P((3))^\circ$ would satisfy $f(mh)=f(m)h$ for every $h$; taking $h=T_i$ and a nonzero $m$ gives $f(-m)=f(m)$ because $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ has $T_i$ acting by $-1$ and $P((3))^\circ$ has $T_i$ acting by $+1$, while $f(-m)=-f(m)$ in characteristic zero, so $-f(m)=f(m)$ forces $f(m)=0$, contradicting injectivity over $\mathbb Q$. Therefore no such isomorphism exists and the untwisted claim is false. The twisted statement is consistent: on $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))^\theta$ the generator $T_i$ acts by the ordinary action of $\theta(T_i)=-T_i$, that is by $+1$, matching $P((3))$, and the unit is $u_{(3)}=1$ by [F2].

derivations.claim: **Shape (3).** For the one-row shape, $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$ and right multiplication by $T_i$ permutes the sum, with the scalar rule $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}$ because every $T_wT_i$ recombines into $q$ times the full sum; since $z_{(3)}=x_{(3)}T_{w_{(3)}}y_{(1^3)}=x_{(3)}$ (here $w_{(3)}=1$ and $y_{(1^3)}=1$) the module $P((3))$ is the free rank-one module on $x_{(3)}$ with action $q$. Squaring gives $x_{(3)}^2=\sum_{v,w}T_vT_w=\sum_vT_vx_{(3)}=\bigl(\sum_vq^{\ell(v)}\bigr)x_{(3)}=p_3(q)x_{(3)}$, because the length distribution in $S_3$ is $(1,2,2,1)$ and $1+2q+2q^2+q^3=(1+q)(1+q+q^2)$; hence the Murphy cell has form value $G_{(3)}(c_{(3)},c_{(3)})=p_3(q)$ and action $q$, and $\beta(x_{(3)},x_{(3)})=1$ by [F1].

**Shape (1^3).** For the one-column shape, $x_{(1^3)}=1$ and $P((1^3))=y_{(3)}H$ with $y_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w$. The pair argument $y_{(3)}T_i=\sum_{u}(-q)^{-\ell(u)}T_{us_i}$ over the two cosets of $\langle s_i\rangle$ gives $y_{(3)}T_i=-y_{(3)}$ for $i=1,2$, the sign representation of the rank-one module. The distinguished basis of $M((1^3))$ is the standard basis and $\beta$ is diagonal with entries $q^{\ell(w)}$, so $\beta(y_{(3)},y_{(3)})=\sum_wq^{-2\ell(w)}q^{\ell(w)}=\sum_wq^{-\ell(w)}=q^{-3}p_3(q)$, the last equality by $w\mapsto w_0w$. Modulo the higher ideal $I^{\rhd(1^3)}$, which contains $1+T_i$ because $1+T_i=x_{(2,1)}$ is a Murphy element of shape $(2,1)$, the class $c_{(1^3)}$ satisfies $T_i=-1$ and $G_{(1^3)}(c_{(1^3)},c_{(1^3)})=P_{(1^3)}(q)=1$ by [F2].

**The comparison maps.** By [F3] applied to $\lambda=(3)$, where $\lambda'=(1^3)$ and $\ell(w_0(S_{(1^3)}))=\ell(w_{(3)})=0$, the isomorphism $\Phi_{(3)}$ has unit $u_{(3)}=1$ and the identity $G^\theta_{(1^3)}(\Phi_{(3)}x_{(3)},\Phi_{(3)}x_{(3)})=\beta(x_{(3)},x_{(3)})=1$ is consistent because both sides are the value of the respective rank-one forms; explicitly $\Phi_{(3)}(x_{(3)})=c_{(1^3)}$ by [F3]. Applying it to $\lambda=(1^3)$, where $\lambda'=(3)$ and $\ell(w_0(S_{(3)}))=3$, $\ell(w_{(1^3)})=0$, gives $u_{(1^3)}=q^3$, and the identity $G_{(3)}(c_{(3)},c_{(3)})=q^3\,q^{-3}p_3(q)=p_3(q)$ is consistent; explicitly $\Phi_{(1^3)}(y_{(3)})=c_{(3)}$. In the target $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))^\theta$ the generator acts by the ordinary action of $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i=-T_i$, hence by $+1=q$ at $q=1$; in the target $C_{\mathrm M}((3))^\theta$ it acts by the ordinary action of $(q-1)-T_i$ on the class acting by $q$, hence by $(q-1)-q=-1$; these match the source actions $q$ on $P((3))$ and $-1$ on $P((1^3))$ computed in steps 1.1 and 1.2.

**Specialization and conclusion.** At $q=1$ over $\mathbb Q$ the four form values become $1$, $1^{-3}p_3(1)=6$, $6$ and $1$, and $\theta$ is the sign automorphism exchanging the trivial and sign modules, in agreement with [F4]; the module actions match as in step 2.1. Every displayed identity is an identity in $A=\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$ between Laurent polynomials, so all of them specialize along any ring map $A\to R$ with $q\mapsto q\in R^\times$. Only the rank-one computations, the trace-free form evaluations and the comparison theorem were used; no choice principle is used.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ be the type-A Hecke algebra over $R$ with generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, quadratic relations $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid and distant
commutation relations, and standard basis $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); here
$\ell(w)$ is the inversion length of $w\in S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). All modules below are right
modules.

**The star anti-involution.** Let $\sigma\mapsto\sigma^*$ be the unique
$R$-algebra anti-automorphism of $H$ with $T_i^*=T_i$ for every generator: it
exists because every defining relator is invariant under reversal of words
(the quadratic relator $T_i^2-(q-1)T_i-q$, the braid relator
$T_iT_{i+1}T_i-T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}$ and each distant commutation relator are
palindromes), so reversal descends from the free algebra to $H$, and it is
unique because the generators generate $H$. On the standard basis
$T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$, since reversing a reduced word for $w$ is a reduced word
for $w^{-1}$.

**Tableau conventions.** Write $t\cdot\sigma$ for the right action of $S_n$ on
tableaux defined by $(t\cdot\sigma)(c):=\sigma^{-1}(t(c))$; it is the inverse
of the left action $(\sigma\cdot t)(c)=\sigma(t(c))$ of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]], and it is a right action.
A $\lambda$-tableau is **row standard** when its entries strictly increase
along every row; columns are not constrained. Let $t^\lambda$ be the row-filled
$\lambda$-tableau, whose row $i$ carries
$\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\dots,\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i$ from left
to right, and let $t_\lambda$ be the column-filled $\lambda$-tableau, whose
column $j$ carries consecutive integers downward; equivalently
$t_\lambda(i,j)=t^{\lambda'}(j,i)$, so that $t_\lambda$ is the transpose of
$t^{\lambda'}$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

**The row subgroup and the coset representatives.** Let $S_\lambda$ be the
**row subgroup** of $\lambda$, the subgroup of $S_n$ preserving every row of
$t^\lambda$; writing
$$B_i:=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+2,\ \dots,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$$
for the $i$-th row block of $t^\lambda$, one has
$S_\lambda=S(B_1)\times\cdots\times S(B_k)$, the direct product of the
symmetric groups of the individual row blocks. Let
$$D_\lambda:=\{d\in S_n:t^\lambda\cdot d\text{ is row standard}\}.$$
This is the set of minimal-length right coset representatives of $S_\lambda$ in
$S_n$: every right coset $S_\lambda d$ has exactly one element $d_0$ for which
$t^\lambda\cdot d_0$ is row standard, and it satisfies
$\ell(wd_0)=\ell(w)+\ell(d_0)$ for all $w\in S_\lambda$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). Let
$w_\lambda\in S_n$ be the unique element with $t^\lambda\cdot w_\lambda=t_\lambda$;
existence and uniqueness hold because the action of $S_n$ on $\lambda$-tableaux
is free and transitive.

**Generators and modules.** For a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ put
$$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w,\qquad y_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w,\qquad z_\lambda:=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_{\lambda'},$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition of $\lambda$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). The **row
permutation module** is the right ideal $M(\lambda):=x_\lambda H\subseteq H$,
and the **ordinary Dipper-James polytabloid module** is
$P(\lambda):=z_\lambda H\subseteq M(\lambda)$; $z_\lambda$ is its polytabloid
generator.

**The forms.** The **permutation form** is the $R$-bilinear form $\beta$ on
$M(\lambda)$ determined on the distinguished family
$\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ by
$$\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}\qquad(d,e\in D_\lambda),$$
and the **DJ form** is the restriction of $\beta$ to $P(\lambda)$. That family
is an $R$-basis of $M(\lambda)$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]), so the displayed
values define a unique bilinear form; the family is $\{x_\varnothing\}=\{1\}$
for the empty partition.

**Small cases and base change.** For $\lambda=\varnothing$ set
$x_\varnothing=y_\varnothing=z_\varnothing=1$, so that
$M(\varnothing)=P(\varnothing)=R$ and $\beta$ is the standard form; for
$n=0,1$ there are no generators and $H=R$. Every base change
$A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$, produces all
objects above over $R$ by the same formulas; the suppliers of this page prove
that the distinguished families and the form are compatible with such base
change. No choice principle is used.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write
$\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let
$P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign
automorphism $\theta$ be as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]],
[[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and
[[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of
[[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules
   $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$
   where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and
   the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$
   and read in the twist; in particular
   $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for
   $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. Moreover
   $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(m)$.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of
   [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and
   $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$,
   $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$
   over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no
   potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit
   $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto
   the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients
   is an isomorphism, and the DJ head corresponds to the twisted Murphy head,
   $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$,
   including the zero-quotient case. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the
   unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their
   reductions. One also obtains
   $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the
   dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign
   transport. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with its basis $\{m_t\}$, $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$,
the permutation form $\beta$ on $M(\lambda)$ and the DJ form on $P(\lambda)$
be as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]],
[[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and
[[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]. Then:

1. Setting $B_\lambda(m_s,p):=\beta(x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(s)},p)$ for
   $s\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$ and $p\in P(\lambda)$ defines an explicit
   $R$-bilinear pairing
   $B_\lambda\colon C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\times P(\lambda)\to R$ that is
   $H$-balanced, $B_\lambda(mh,p)=B_\lambda(m,ph^*)$, and whose adjoint
   $c\mapsto B_\lambda(c,-)$ is an isomorphism of right $H$-modules
   $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$ onto the star-contragredient
   module of [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. No
   nondegeneracy of the DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ is required.

2. Equivalently, the kernel of the quotient map
   $M(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is the orthogonal complement
   $P(\lambda)^\perp=\{a\in M(\lambda):\beta(a,p)=0\text{ for all }p\in P(\lambda)\}$,
   and its preimage under the quotient is
   $M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$; the pairing matrices in the bases
   $\{m_s\}$ and $\{e_t\}$ have entries $B_\lambda(m_s,e_t)=q^{\ell(d_\lambda(s))}a_{t,d_\lambda(s)}$
   and determinant a unit of $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$.

3. All statements are compatible with every base change $A\to R$,
   $v\mapsto q$; the construction uses no generic semisimplicity, no
   nondegeneracy of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ and no choice principle.

derivations.claim: **Row module.** From [F1], $b_0T_1=xT_1=qx=q\,b_0$, $b_1T_1=xT_2T_1=b_2$ and $b_2T_1=xT_2T_1^2=xT_2((q-1)T_1+q)=(q-1)b_2+q\,b_1$; also $b_0T_2=b_1$, $b_1T_2=xT_2^2=x((q-1)T_2+q)=(q-1)b_1+q\,b_0$ and $b_2T_2=xT_2T_1T_2=xT_1T_2T_1=q\,xT_2T_1=q\,b_2$, using the braid relation. In the basis $(b_0,b_1,b_2)$ with coordinate row vectors these are exactly the matrices $R_1$ and $R_2$ of the statement, and $\beta(b_i,b_i)=q^{i}$ by [F2] because $\ell(1)=0$, $\ell(s_2)=1$, $\ell(s_2s_1)=2$.

**Polytabloids and their form.** Since $z_\lambda=xT_2(1-q^{-1}T_1)$ by [F4] and $y_{\lambda'}=1-q^{-1}T_1$, the displayed expressions $p_0=b_1-q^{-1}b_2$ and $p_1=zT_2=b_1T_2-q^{-1}b_2T_2=qb_0+(q-1)b_1-b_2$ follow from step 1.1. Their coordinates on $(b_0,b_2)$ give the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-q^{-1}\\q&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $q\cdot q^{-1}=1$, a unit over every $R$; hence the two polytabloids span a free rank-two split submodule stable under both generators, which by the comparison theorem is exactly $P(\lambda)=zH$. Weighted inner products against the diagonal form of [F2] give $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}q+1&q^2\\q^2&q^3+q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$: explicitly $B_{00}=q+q^{-2}\cdot q^2=q+1$, $B_{01}=(q-1)q+q^2$ ... computing $(b_1-q^{-1}b_2,qb_0+(q-1)b_1-b_2)$ term by term gives $q(q-1)+q=q^2$, and $B_{11}=q^2+(q-1)^2q+q^2=q^3+q$. Its determinant is $q(q^2+q+1)$.

**The Murphy quotient.** In $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ the higher vector $x_{(3)}=b_0+b_1+b_2$ vanishes by [F3], so $b_2=-c_0-c_1$ and $c_1=xT_2=b_1$. Then $c_0T_1=qx=q\,c_0$ and $c_1T_1=b_2=-c_0-c_1$, giving $M_1$; also $c_0T_2=c_1$ and $c_1T_2=(q-1)b_1+qb_0=(q-1)c_1+qc_0$, giving $M_2$. Expanding the defining products of [F3] in the Murphy basis and reading the coefficient of $m_{t_0t_0}=x$ gives $G(c_0,c_0)=q+1$ from $x^2=(q+1)x$, $G(c_0,c_1)=-1$ and $G(c_1,c_1)=q^2+1$; equivalently $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}q+1&-1\\-1&q^2+1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $q^3+q^2+q$.

**Comparison, cross-pairing and specializations.** The comparison theorem of [F4] gives $\Phi(z)=c_0$, hence $\Phi(p_1)=\Phi(zT_2)=c_0\theta(T_2)=(q-1)c_0-c_1$ and $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\q-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$; direct matrix multiplication verifies $P_iA=A((q-1)I-M_i)$ for $i=1,2$ and $AGA^{\mathsf T}=B$, the latter being the form identity with the unit $u_\lambda=1$. The cross-pairing entries $B_\lambda(c_s,p_t)=\beta(b_{d(s)},p_t)$ on the standard bases give $Q=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&q\\q&q(q-1)\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $\det Q=-q^2\in A^\times$, so the pairing is perfect as in [F4]. The two Gram determinants agree with $q(1+q+q^2)$. At $q=-1$ in characteristic zero, $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&-2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ have determinant $-1$, although $[2]_q=1+q=0$; at $q=1$ in characteristic $2$, both reduce to $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $1$, hence with zero radical. All identities are Laurent-polynomial identities, so they specialize to every $R$; no choice principle is used.
